content: The vaccine efficacy against clinical malaria (both uncomplicated and severe) in older children was 51% (95% CI: 47-55) during the 12 months following the administration of the first three doses, as determined by per-protocol analysis. Children aged 5 to 17 months were randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) a group receiving sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine and amodiaquine (SMC, the chemoprevention-alone group), (2) a group receiving RTS,S/AS01E (the vaccine-alone group), or (3) a group receiving both chemoprevention and RTS,S/AS01E (the combination group). Severe malaria was assessed based on the presence of Plasmodium falciparum asexual parasitemia at a density of >5000 parasites per cubic millimeter, along with one or more markers of disease severity, and without evidence of coexisting illnesses. Markers of severe disease included prostration, respiratory distress, a Blantyre coma score of 2 (on a scale of 0 to 5, with higher scores indicating better consciousness), two or more seizures, hypoglycemia, acidosis, elevated lactate levels, or hemoglobin levels <5 g/dL. Coexisting illnesses were defined as radiographically confirmed pneumonia, meningitis diagnosed via cerebrospinal fluid analysis, bacteremia, or gastroenteritis with severe dehydration. The 4-dose group received three doses of RTS,S/AS01 at months 0, 1, and 2, followed by a booster dose at month 20. The control group received a comparator vaccine at the same time points. Protective efficacy was calculated as (1 hazard ratio). A pilot implementation study was conducted using a cluster-randomized control methodology. Across three countries, there were 27,678 admissions to sentinel hospitals among children aged 1-59 months during the period from vaccine introduction to April 30, 2021. Of these, 4853 admissions were vaccine-eligible based on birth date in areas where the vaccine was provided (implementing areas), compared to 5141 vaccine-eligible admissions in comparison areas. Among children eligible to have received all three primary doses of RTS,S/AS01, there were 1107 admissions with severe malaria out of 9994 total age-eligible admissions, with 418 from implementing areas and 689 from comparison areas. Among children not eligible for the vaccine, there were 2703 admissions with severe malaria out of 17,684 total age-ineligible admissions, with 1313 from implementing areas and 1390 from comparison areas. Severe malaria anemia was the most common form of severe malaria, with 25 out of 37 cases in the vaccine group and 31 out of 37 cases in the SMC group. The risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias were all assessed as not serious. However, imprecision was considered serious or very serious in several analyses due to the small number of events and wide confidence intervals, which included the possibility of both benefit and harm. Patients admitted to sentinel hospitals were routinely tested for malaria infection using rapid diagnostic tests (RDT) or microscopy. Among the 27,678 total admissions, test results were available for 88%. Among children eligible to have received three vaccine doses, 2630 admissions tested positive for malaria, with 1075 from implementing areas and 1555 from comparison areas. The study design and analysis were carefully scrutinized by independent experts, and despite heavy involvement of the funder, the study was considered well-conducted. However, some outcomes were not pre-specified in the protocol, leading to concerns about post-hoc analysis. The WHO guidelines for malaria, updated on October 16, 2023, reflect these findings and emphasize the importance of continued evaluation of vaccine efficacy and implementation strategies.
